snapshot.title: TNPSC Unit 8: Imperial Cholas — Power & Art
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ TNPSC Unit 8 Hook: Chola: Thanjavur. Raja Raja: Big Temple. Rajendra: Ganges. Uttiramerur: Admin. Kudavolai: Election. Nataraja: Bronze.

quick_notes.title: Founder
quick_notes.detail: Vijayalaya Chola (850 AD) captured Thanjavur from Muttaraiyars.
quick_notes.explanation: The founder of the medieval Chola Empire was Vijayalaya Chola. Around the year 850 AD, he captured the city of Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars, who were a local ruling clan in present-day Tamil Nadu. The Cholas were a powerful dynasty in South India, and Thanjavur became their first major capital. Vijayalaya’s victory marked the beginning of a new Chola kingdom that would later grow into a vast empire. The term Muttaraiyars refers to a group of chiefs who controlled parts of the Kaveri delta before Vijayalaya defeated them.

quick_notes.title: Raja Raja I (The Great)
quick_notes.detail: Built Brihadeeswarar Temple (Thanjavur). Title : Mummidi Cholan. Naval conquest of Sri Lanka and Maldives.
quick_notes.explanation: Raja Raja I, also known as Raja Raja the Great, was a powerful king of the Chola dynasty in South India. He is most famous for building the Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur, which is a massive Hindu temple made of granite and a UNESCO World Heritage site. His official title was Mummidi Cholan, which means "the Chola who wears three crowns," symbolizing his rule over three kingdoms. He expanded his empire by conquering northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives islands using a strong navy, which is a country's fleet of warships. A navy is the part of a country's military that fights at sea. This naval conquest made the Chola Empire one of the most powerful maritime, or sea-based, empires of its time.

quick_notes.title: Rajendra I
quick_notes.detail: "Gangaikonda Cholan". Founded Gangaikondacholapuram. Naval expedition to Srivijaya (SE Asia).
quick_notes.explanation: Rajendra I was a powerful king of the Chola dynasty in South India who ruled from around 1014 to 1044 CE. He is famously known as "Gangaikonda Cholan," which means "the Chola who conquered the Ganges," because he led a successful military campaign northward to the Ganges River. After this victory, he founded a new capital city called Gangaikondacholapuram, which translates to "the city of the Chola who conquered the Ganges." He also launched a major naval expedition, meaning a military operation using ships, to the kingdom of Srivijaya, which was located in Southeast Asia (modern-day Indonesia and Malaysia). This naval campaign was one of the earliest examples of Indian military power projecting across the ocean, and it helped the Chola empire control trade routes in the region.

quick_notes.title: Local Administration
quick_notes.detail: Uttiramerur Inscription (Parantaka I) explains the Kudavolai system (lucky draw for village council).
quick_notes.explanation: The Uttiramerur Inscription, created during the reign of Parantaka I, a Chola king, describes the Kudavolai system, which was a method for selecting members of a village council. In this system, the names of eligible candidates were written on palm leaves, placed in a pot, and then drawn out one by one, similar to a lucky draw or lottery, to ensure fair and random selection. This process, called Kudavolai, meaning "pot and draw" in Tamil, was used to choose representatives for local administration, such as managing water tanks, temples, and roads. The inscription shows that ancient villages in South India had a structured, democratic way of electing their local leaders, where every candidate had an equal chance of being chosen.

quick_notes.title: Chola Art
quick_notes.detail: Big Temple (Thanjavur), Airavateswara (Darasuram). Famous Chola Bronzes (Nataraja).
quick_notes.explanation: The Chola dynasty, which ruled parts of South India from around 850 to 1250 AD, created two main types of art: stone temples and metal statues. The most famous Chola temple is the Brihadeeswara Temple, also called the Big Temple, located in Thanjavur, which was built by King Raja Raja Chola I and is known for its massive 216-foot-tall tower. Another important Chola temple is the Airavateswara Temple in Darasuram, built by King Rajaraja Chola II, which is smaller but has very detailed stone carvings. The Cholas are also famous for their bronze sculptures, especially the statue of Nataraja, which shows the Hindu god Shiva dancing inside a ring of fire and represents the cycle of creation and destruction. These bronze statues were made using a method called lost-wax casting, where a wax model is covered in clay, heated to melt the wax out, and then filled with molten metal to create a solid figure. Both the temples and the bronzes are recognized as UNESCO World Heritage sites for their artistic and historical importance.

In TNPSC, 'Local Administration (Uttiramerur)' and 'Chola Bronze' are the most frequent topics. From Raja Raja's Big Temple to the Naval expeditions to Sumatra—this is the legendary Chola era. Do you know which inscription describes the 'Kudavolai' system? Let's master the Cholas today.
